transcript.text: my tumble dryer is giving off a burning smell?? is it safe to keep using it

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A burning smell from a tumble dryer can be a fire risk. The most common cause is fluff/lint restricting airflow and allowing the heater area to overheat. Other possibilities are a slipping drive belt or motor fault, or an internal electrical fault; those need inspection rather than another test cycle. With it cold, switched off and unplugged:
1. Remove and thoroughly clean the door lint filter. Check for lint around its housing without poking tools inside.
2. If it is a condenser or heat-pump dryer, remove the lower filter/condenser only as the handbook permits and clear visible fluff. Let any rinsed part dry before refitting.
3. If it has an external vent hose, check it is not crushed, kinked or visibly blocked. If there has been smoke, melting, scorch marks, or a strong acrid/electrical smell, keep it isolated and tell the engineer that specifically.
ok i've switched it off at the wall already?? the lint filter is really full, i haven't cleaned it in a few weeks. the hose behind is squashed and i can see fluff inside the end of it. is that bad??

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes — that is bad, and it is a very credible reason for the burning smell. A full lint filter plus a squashed, fluff-filled hose restricts airflow, so heat cannot escape properly and the dryer can overheat. Clean the filter and have the vent hose cleared, shortened/re-routed if needed so it is not crushed, and check the outside vent flap/grille is clear. Do this only with the dryer cold, switched off and unplugged; avoid pushing tools deep into the machine. However, because there has already been a burning smell, do not use it again after cleaning or run a test cycle. It needs a qualified engineer to inspect it for lint build-up around hot internal parts and for heat or electrical damage. The airflow restriction is the leading cause, but the inspection is needed to rule out a damaged thermostat/thermal cut-out, wiring, motor or belt. With it cold, isolated and unplugged, can you see any scorch marks, melting or smoke residue around the filter area or at the vent-hose connection?
no scorch marks or smoke that i can see?? the plug felt warm but not hot, is that ok?? it's a Beko and it's in a cupboard with the door shut, and there's a laundry basket on top of it

A plug should generally stay cool. Slight warmth can happen under a heavy load, but in the context of a burning smell it is not something to treat as OK or continue using. The packed lint filter, crushed fluff-filled hose, shut cupboard and basket on top all point strongly to restricted airflow and overheating. The warm plug also leaves a possible plug/socket connection problem to rule out. Keep the dryer isolated and arrange an engineer inspection; do not run it after cleaning as a test. 1. Leave the cupboard door open and remove the basket from the top, so the appliance has ventilation. This does not make it safe to use yet.
2. Once fully cold and unplugged, clean the lint filter and have the vent hose and outside vent properly cleared and rerouted so it cannot be squashed.
3. Inspect the unplugged plug and the wall socket externally only. Any browning, melting, looseness or burnt smell means do not use that socket either and have an electrician check it as well as the dryer. Even with no visible scorching around the filter or hose connection, the burning smell after that level of airflow restriction warrants an engineer checking for internal lint build-up and heat damage.
[Safety panel] Overheating can be a fire risk. Clean the lint filter and make sure the airflow/vent isn't blocked, and don't leave the dryer running unattended. If it smells of burning, stop using it and unplug it.
